title: Does It Cost Anything to Transfer Your Florida Real Estate License?
metaDesc: The DBPR change of broker itself is free. Here's what actually can cost you money when you switch brokerages in Florida, and what doesn't.
h1: Does It Cost Anything to Transfer Your Florida Real Estate License?
about: What it actually costs, if anything, to change your employing broker on a Florida real estate license
answer: No. Changing your employing broker with the Florida DBPR (form RE 11) carries no state fee. It's a free record update, not a new license application. The costs that can show up when you switch brokerages come from somewhere else entirely: your local Realtor board or MLS membership transfer, and whatever your new brokerage charges for desk fees or onboarding, not from the state.
takeaways: The DBPR's change of broker form (RE 11) has no fee. This is the most common myth agents ask about before switching.
Any real cost to switching comes from your local Realtor board or MLS, not the state. Confirm their specific transfer process directly, since it varies by board.
Your new brokerage may have its own onboarding or desk fee structure, separate from anything DBPR-related.
A short overlap in board or MLS dues is possible if your old and new memberships don't line up perfectly. Ask both boards how they handle a mid-cycle switch.
None of this changes your license number or your standing with the state. Only your employing broker of record updates.
tldr: Transferring your Florida real estate license to a new broker doesn't cost anything at the state level. The DBPR's change of broker form is free. Any real expense comes from your local Realtor board or MLS membership transfer, or from your new brokerage's own onboarding fees, so check with those directly rather than assuming the state charges you.
body:
Is there a state fee to switch brokers in Florida?

No. The Florida DBPR processes a change of employing broker through form RE 11, and that transaction carries no state fee. You're not applying for a new license or paying to reissue anything. You're updating a single field on your existing record: who you're currently registered under. This surprises a lot of agents, since switching jobs almost always costs something in other industries.

So where does the idea of a transfer fee come from?

Some confusion comes from mixing up the DBPR change of broker with other, unrelated transactions that do carry small fees, like reprinting a physical license or certain address changes. Those are separate from a broker change and don't apply just because you're switching firms. If you see a dollar figure attached to "license transfer" anywhere, confirm exactly which transaction it's describing before assuming it applies to your situation.

What can actually cost you money when you switch?

The real costs sit outside the DBPR entirely. Your local Realtor board and MLS (not the state) typically require you to update your membership when you change brokerages, and some boards structure dues or transfer processes differently than others. If your old and new memberships don't align perfectly on timing, you can end up covering a short overlap. This is worth a direct call to your board rather than a guess, since it genuinely varies.

What about desk fees or onboarding costs?

Separately from anything DBPR or board related, your new brokerage may have its own cost structure: desk fees, technology fees, or a graduated commission split while you ramp up. These are brokerage-specific business terms, not government fees, and they're worth asking about directly and in writing before you commit to a move.

What doesn't change when you switch brokers

Your license number, your years of experience, and your standing with the state all stay exactly the same. A broker change is an administrative update, not a reset. The only thing that resets, in a sense, is your desk: your new brokerage's tools, splits, and support structure, which is the part actually worth comparing before you decide where to go.

Switching to Adams, Cameron & Co.

If you're weighing a move to Adams, Cameron & Co., the largest brokerage in Volusia and Flagler counties since 1963, a non-competing manager will walk you through exactly what your board transfer looks like and what our own fee structure is, in writing, before you decide anything. Start a confidential conversation.

Fee schedules are set by the DBPR, local Realtor boards, and individual brokerages, and can change. Confirm current requirements directly with those organizations. Educational only, not legal or financial advice.

faq.q: Does the DBPR charge a fee to change brokers in Florida?
faq.a: No. The change of employing broker (form RE 11) is a free transaction with the state. You're updating a record, not applying for a new license.

faq.q: Why do some sources mention a transfer fee?
faq.a: That figure usually describes a different, unrelated DBPR transaction, like reprinting a license or an address change, not the broker change itself. Confirm exactly which transaction a fee applies to before assuming it's part of switching brokers.

faq.q: What actually can cost money when I switch brokerages?
faq.a: Your local Realtor board or MLS membership transfer, and your new brokerage's own desk fees or onboarding costs. Neither of those comes from the state, and both vary, so confirm directly.

faq.q: Can I owe dues to two boards at once during a switch?
faq.a: It's possible if your old and new memberships don't line up on timing. Ask both boards how they handle a mid-cycle change so you know what to expect.

faq.q: Does switching brokers affect my license number or standing?
faq.a: No. Your license number and standing with the state stay the same. Only your employing broker of record updates.

ctaSub: A non-competing Adams, Cameron & Co. manager will show you exactly what changes, and what doesn't, in writing.
